newsitem.title: CHINA: FOCUS-China share market moves ring in changes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-China share market moves ring in changes.

text.p: China's ban on state bank funds flowing into shares could ring in fundamental changes for the country's stock markets, transforming the casinos of old into credible and stable exchanges, analysts said on Friday.
But the changes will not be painless, they said, as Chinese investors have yet to come to grips with the idea that stocks can be vehicles for long-term investment as well as quick profits.
Values on China's two stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen rose more than 50 percent between the start of 1997 and May.
The latest ban, announced late on Thursday, should finally see China's young exchanges begin to develop into credible retail markets, they said.
"China's stock markets had become somewhat like casino floors in the first few months of this year," said one executive with a major Chinese brokerage.
"Now, with the recent series of measures, they are expected to gradually establish the function of investment," he said.

The People's Bank of China, the central bank, issued an urgent directive after the markets closed on Thursday banning state banks from trading on the stock markets and giving them 10 days to unwind their positions.
The central bank also barred state banks from trading on the state debt repurchase and spot secondary markets from Friday.
China in May introduced measures to cool the stock markets, including a huge 30 billion yuan new share quota for 1997.
Analysts said the new measures, the most serious yet in the Chinese government's attempts to bring some order to the share markets, could see liquidity cut by up to half.
Only securities houses and trust and investment firms will be left to trade on the two bourses, they said. Insurance firms have always been barred.
"Fundamental changes will occur, with retail investors expected to account for a greater proportion of stock trading," a Shanghai trader said.
"The withdrawal of large numbers of speculative institutional investors will sharply cut the speculative element on the stock markets," said an analyst with a brokerage in Jiangsu province.
"This will benefit the market in long run," he said.
Institutions such as state banks in collaboration with some securities houses and listed firms had been major speculators, an editorial in the central bank's Financial News said on Friday.
"A handful of commercial (state) banks and their branches had directly bought shares using bank money or had offered credit to securities brokerages to buy new shares," it said.
Analysts said the process of cooling down the markets would not be without problems. But the markets are only six years old, they noted, and growing up is never easy.
"The stock markets have so far been dominated by institutional investors with prices moving up and down sharply from time to time," said a broker.
"Retail investors will find themselves at a loss if prices move slowly for a long time," he said.
"They have yet to become familiar with the idea of stock investment instead of speculation."
Traders said the domestic currency A share indices could lose around 20 percent from Thursday's close due to the ban.
The foreign currency B share indices, while not as vulnerable because they are dominated by foreign funds, could shed eight to 10 percent before the markets stabilise, the trading sources said.
"The market needs at least two weeks to offset the negative impact of the latest ban," said an analyst in Shenzhen.
On Friday, Shanghai's domestic A shares plunged 6.3 percent and the B share index fell 4.34 percent. The Shenzhen A share index plummeted 6.83 percent and the B index shed 3.83 percent.
